crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: The threshold of machine authorship is the line between a human created work and an output that a copyright system will treat as authorless.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities and AI fiduciaries sit at the meeting point of agency law, fiduciary duty, corporate governance, and AI regulation.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: Liability when agents interact covers the legal questions that arise when two or more autonomous or semi-autonomous AI agents exchange instructions, negotiate, transact, or act on shared systems and a loss, breach, or injury follows.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes and evidentiary standards concerns how courts, tribunals, arbitrators, and regulators decide whether a synthetic or manipulated audio, image, or video can be admitted, authenticated, and weighed as evidence.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation is a legal claim that a person can ask for the logic behind an automated decision that affects them.

sections.body: This field deals with legal questions that appear when AI systems write, decide, negotiate, or act through multiple agents. It is not about whether AI can be a lawyer in a courtroom drama. It is about authorship, fiduciary duty, shared liability, evidence, and explanation. Courts and regulators are now handling disputes over AI-generated works, autonomous trading or contracting entities, and chains of agents that cause harm. The work is practical: drafting rules, testing evidence, and deciding who must answer when a machine acts. The pages here examine those questions as they arise in live disputes and regulatory proposals.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are more settled than others. Copyright offices and courts have begun to require human authorship for certain protections, but the line between assistance and authorship remains contested. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows that litigation is real but still thin in many areas. Multi-agent liability is largely unresolved because causation can be distributed across software, data, and human operators, and deepfake evidence challenges authentication rules that assume a recording can be traced to a source. The right to an explanation is recognized in some data protection regimes, yet the technical and legal standards for a meaningful explanation are not stable. The honest limit is that most frameworks are emerging, not complete, and many questions will be answered by settlements, agency guidance, or state bills rather than definitive high court rulings.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section move from creation to conduct to proof to process. The Threshold of Machine Authorship is the starting point for questions about who owns or can protect AI-generated output. Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries looks at whether an AI system or the people behind it owe duties when it manages money, data, or decisions. Liability When Agents Interact addresses the harder problem of harm caused by several AI agents or humans working together. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards is for readers who need to understand how courts test manipulated audio, video, and images. The Right to an Explanation covers the demand that a person receive reasons for an automated decision, and read together these pages show how authorship, entity status, shared causation, evidence, and explanation form one connected legal problem.
